entries.type: direction; also particle — the second word of many phrasal verbs (give up, eat up)
entries.position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but always after a pronoun (pick it up)
entries.modifies: verbs, especially verbs of motion; phrasal verbs
entries.contrast: With an object after it, up is a preposition (walk up the hill); with none, it is the adverb (look up). As a particle it can come before or after a noun object (pick up the box, pick the box up) but must follow a pronoun: pick it up, never pick up it. Very often up does not mean вверх at all but ‘completely’, like a Russian perfective prefix: eat up = съесть, use up = израсходовать, drink up = допить. What's up? and Time's up are adjective uses.

entries.contrast: down the street is the preposition and means ‘along, по улице’, not ‘downhill’. The pronoun goes before the particle: write it down, never write down it. I feel down (мне грустно) is an adjective. Down to Texas and up to Chicago for south and north are everyday American speech, even across flat land.

entries.position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (hand it in)
entries.modifies: verbs, especially verbs of motion; phrasal verbs
entries.contrast: Russian в covers three English forms: come in (adverb, no object), come into the room (preposition into, movement) and be in the room (preposition in, location). Come in the house is common in American speech, but into is the standard for movement. in meaning ‘fashionable’ (Wide jeans are in) is an adjective.

entries.contrast: Don't confuse with inwardly, which means ‘privately, in one's mind’: Inwardly, she was furious = в душе. The adjective goes before a noun: inward calm. American inward, British also inwards.

examples: The storm is moving northward along the coast.

entries.position: end — after the verb
entries.contrast: In everyday American speech the plain compass word is the adverb: drive north, head north, up north. northward sounds written or technical. No to before the bare word: go north, but to the north.

entries.position: end — after the verb

examples: The storm system is moving eastward across the plains.

entries.position: end — after the verb
entries.contrast: In speech Americans say drive east, head east; eastward sounds written. back East in American speech means ‘in the eastern United States’. No to before the bare word: go east, but to the east.

examples: Settlers pushed westward in the 1800s.

entries.position: end — after the verb
entries.contrast: In speech Americans say drive west, head west; westward is written and historical (westward expansion, the 19th-century settlement of the American West, uses the adjective). No to before the bare word: go west, but to the west.

examples: We finally started homeward after midnight.

entries.meaning: In the direction the hands of a clock move. ---

examples: Vinyl records have been around for over a century.
Smartphones weren't around when I was a kid.

senses.head: Without a purpose, doing nothing useful
examples: We just sat around all afternoon.
Stop fooling around and do your homework.

senses.head: By a longer route, not directly
examples: The bridge was closed, so we had to go around.
We took the long way around.

senses.head: So that each person gets a share
examples: Is there enough cake to go around?
They passed the photos around.

senses.head: To a new opinion, especially one first rejected (in come around)
examples: She hated the idea at first, but she came around.
Give him time; he'll come around.

senses.head: In circumference, measured all the way around
examples: The trunk of the old oak is nearly ten feet around.
How big around is your wrist?

entries.type: direction; also place, degree (around 50) and particle
entries.position: end; before a number when it means ‘about’
entries.contrast: American English uses around where British often says round (turn around, go around) or about (around 50 people, walk around). Meaning ‘about’, it goes before the number: around six, never six around. With an object it is a preposition: around the corner.

senses.head: Remaining, not used

senses.head: More than a stated amount, age, or time

senses.head: Carefully, from beginning to end

Look the contract over before you sign.

senses.head: To another person, side, or system
examples: Hand over the keys.

senses.head: Everywhere (in all over)
examples: I've looked all over for my glasses.
Students came from all over to study there.

entries.type: direction; also frequency (start over) and particle
entries.position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (think it over)
entries.modifies: verbs; phrasal verbs; numbers (65 and over)
entries.contrast: American start over and do it over mean ‘again, заново’ — British says start again. The game is over (закончилась) is an adjective. With an object over is a preposition (over the bridge). come over means ‘come to visit’, not перейти.

Read the contract through before you sign.

Only four teams made it through to the finals.
I tried calling, but I couldn't get through.
Hold on, I'll put you through.

senses.head: In at one side or end and out at the other
examples: The gate was open, so we walked right through.
Move over and let the ambulance through.
Is the road still closed, or can we get through?

senses.head: From the beginning to the end
examples: Read the contract through before you sign.
You didn't think this through.
The baby slept through until six.

senses.head: Successfully past a test, stage, or obstacle

senses.head: Connected by telephone

senses.head: All the way to the final destination, without changing

entries.type: direction; also particle (think through, get through)
entries.position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (think it through)
entries.contrast: American Monday through Friday is a preposition meaning ‘up to and including’ (по пятницу включительно); British says to. I'm through (American) is an adjective meaning ‘I'm finished’. Spelling trap: through θruː, though ðoʊ, thorough ˈθɜːroʊ; thru is informal American. For через over a surface, use across.

entries.type: direction; also particle (turn off, pay off)
entries.position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (turn it off)
entries.contrast: off ɔːf and of əv are different words. American speech often says off of (get off of the couch), but careful writing uses off alone. turn off = выключить, turn down = убавить or отказать. I'm off means ‘I'm leaving’; off meaning ‘not fresh’ or ‘wrong’ (The milk is off) is an adjective.

entries.type: direction; also time (from now on) and particle
entries.position: end — after the verb; with a phrasal verb, before or after a noun object but after a pronoun (put it on)
entries.contrast: put on is the action (надеть); wear or have on is the state (быть в чём-то): She put on a coat, She had a coat on. from now on needs the on: never from now I'll…. What's on tonight? and The game is still on are adjective uses. With an object on is a preposition: on the table.

Is there a gas station close by?
She stood by, watching.

senses.head: Past, going beyond someone or something
examples: A truck roared by.
Days went by and still no news.
Excuse me, can I get by?

senses.head: To someone's home or office, for a short visit
examples: Stop by my office after lunch.
Come by anytime.

senses.head: Managing to live or cope with what one has (in get by)
examples: We get by on one income.
My Spanish is good enough to get by.
How does anyone get by on minimum wage?

senses.head: Near, close at hand
examples: Is there a gas station close by?
She stood by, watching.

senses.head: Ready and waiting (in stand by)
examples: Please stand by for further instructions.

entries.type: direction; also place and particle (stop by, stand by)
entries.position: end — after the verb
entries.contrast: by is far more often a preposition (by bus, by Friday, written by); the adverb has no object after it. stop by and come by mean a short visit, not ‘stop nearby’. stand by can mean ‘wait, ready’ (Please stand by) or ‘watch without acting’. Homophones: buy, bye.

entries.meaning: Going by and beyond a person or place without stopping. ---
examples: A bus went past without stopping.
He walked right past and didn't say hi.
Summer flew past, and the kids were back in school.
entries.position: end — after a verb of motion or of time passing
entries.modifies: verbs of motion and of time passing
entries.contrast: Spelling trap: passed is the past tense of pass (A car passed us); past is the adverb or preposition (A car went past). Both sound the same. half past two and past the bank are prepositions.

It wasn't his fault; it was the other way round.

senses.head: In a circle, turning again and again (in round and round)
examples: The kids spun round and round on the carousel.

senses.head: Through the whole year (in all year round)

senses.head: In the reverse way (in the other way round)
examples: It wasn't his fault; it was the other way round.

entries.position: end — after the verb or at the end of a set phrase
entries.form: the short form of around, kept in a few set phrases
entries.contrast: In American English around is the normal adverb: turn around, go around, come around, the other way around. round survives in round and round and all year round (also year-round); the other way round is still met in American reading but sounds British. British come round for dinner is American come over.

examples: The hikers pushed onward through the snow.

senses.head: Forward, farther along a route
examples: The hikers pushed onward through the snow.
After lunch we drove onward to Denver.

senses.head: Forward in time from a stated point
examples: From the 1990s onward, the city grew fast.
The museum is open from 9 a.m. onward.

entries.position: end — after a verb of motion, or after from + a time
entries.modifies: verbs of motion; time phrases after from
entries.contrast: American onward, British onwards. from 2010 on and from 2010 onward mean the same; don't stack them. Onward and upward! is a set cheer meaning ‘keep going and improving’.

entries.meaning: Up a slope, toward the top of a hill. ---
examples: We pushed our bikes uphill.
The trail climbs uphill for two miles.
Water doesn't flow uphill.
entries.position: end — after the verb
entries.contrast: As an adverb the stress falls on hill; as an adjective before a noun it moves forward, and the adjective is also the figurative one: an uphill battle (тяжёлая борьба).

examples: The kids raced downhill on their sleds.

senses.head: Down a slope
examples: The kids raced downhill on their sleds.
The road runs downhill to the lake.

senses.head: Into a worse condition
examples: After he lost his job, things went downhill fast.
The restaurant has gone downhill since the new owners took over.

entries.position: end — after the verb
entries.contrast: It's all downhill from here is an adjective use after be, and it can mean ‘it gets easier now’ or ‘it only gets worse now’ — context decides. go downhill on its own always means ‘get worse’. As an adjective before a noun the stress moves forward: downhill skiing.

senses.head: Against the current, toward the source of a river
examples: Salmon swim upstream to spawn.

senses.head: At or toward an earlier stage of a process or supply chain
examples: It's cheaper to fix the problem upstream, before the parts reach the factory.
Most of these errors start further upstream.

entries.position: end — after the verb
entries.contrast: In American business and software writing upstream means ‘at an earlier stage’ or ‘at the source a project comes from’, and downstream ‘at a later stage’; the river picture is usually gone.

senses.head: With the current, away from the source of a river

senses.head: At or toward a later stage of a process
examples: A mistake in the design causes bigger problems downstream.

entries.position: end — after the verb
entries.contrast: In American business and software writing downstream means ‘at a later stage’ or ‘affected by an earlier step’, the opposite of upstream; the river picture is usually gone.

entries.meaning: Onto the shore or the bottom of shallow water, so that a ship cannot move. ---

senses.head: To excess, further than is sensible (in go overboard)
examples: Don't go overboard with the decorations.

senses.head: Over the side of a boat or ship into the water
examples: He fell overboard and had to be rescued.

examples: The plan was thrown overboard when the budget was cut.

entries.position: end — after the verb
entries.modifies: verbs of motion; go and throw
entries.form: over + board (the side of a ship)
entries.contrast: go overboard is everyday informal English for doing too much (перебарщивать), and is far more common than the literal sense.
